155.title: Removing a stone from the road
155.hook: taking harm out of a path is a branch of faith (Muslim)
155.tomorrow: Camp 3 close: a day with the practices
155.howItsDone: Muslims count removing anything harmful from a road or path, a stone, glass, a branch, as an act of faith and charity, following the hadith of the branches of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the neighbor, urged by Jibril until an heir seemed near. Your line was start next door. Today, charity as small as it gets. Day one hundred fifty-five.

There's a broken bottle in the middle of the sidewalk. Or a branch across the bike lane. Or a shopping cart abandoned in a parking space. You could step around it. Everyone else has. All week, charity has gotten a little smaller and a little closer: a smile, a secret gift, a welcome for someone new, eight addresses, a well that keeps flowing, the house next door. Today it gets as small as it goes. Today: removing a stone from the road.
screen: `A BROKEN BOTTLE ON THE SIDEWALK.` → `EVERYONE ELSE STEPPED AROUND IT.` → `A WEEK OF CHARITY, SMALLER EACH DAY.`

segments.voice: Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: faith has seventy-some branches, or sixty-some; the narrator wasn't sure which. The highest is saying la ilaha illallah, there is no god but Allah. The lowest is removing something harmful from the road. And modesty is a branch of faith. Put those side by side: the testimony at the center of Islam, the words you met on day one hundred seventeen, and moving a stone out of the way. Same tree, different branches. The smallest act is still faith, not a lesser thing to be embarrassed about. Bukhari and Muslim tell a story about it. A man walking along a road found a thorny branch lying across it, and moved it aside. That's all. And the Prophet said Allah thanked him for it, and forgave him. In another report in Muslim, the Prophet said he saw a man moving about freely in Paradise because of a tree he had cut away from the middle of a road, where it had been hurting people. A companion named Abu Barzah once asked the Prophet: teach me something that will benefit me. The answer, in Sahih Muslim, wasn't a long devotion. It was: remove what harms from the path of the Muslims. Notice who benefits: people you'll never meet. The cyclist who won't swerve. The child who won't cut a foot. The old man who won't trip. They won't thank you, because they'll never know anything was there. It's secret charity, done with your feet. Faith, at its smallest, is noticing the thing in the way, and moving it.
screen: `SEVENTY-SOME BRANCHES OF FAITH.` · `THE HIGHEST AND THE LOWEST.` · `THE THORNY BRANCH, FORGIVEN.` · `TEACH ME SOMETHING THAT HELPS.` · then, large: `CLEAR THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Picture the paths near you: your hallway, your front step, the sidewalk, a shared kitchen, the stairs at work. Notice what's in the way, a box on the stairs, shoes in the doorway, a spill no one wiped, and how many small harms you usually step around without seeing. If you pray, you can intend moving one of them as a branch of faith.
Thorny branch. The hadith's man who moved one off the road, and was thanked and forgiven by Allah for it.
Your line: clear the path. The lowest branch is still on the tree. Day one hundred fifty-five, done.

156.title: Camp 3 close: a day with the practices
156.hook: a whole day shaped by prayer, dhikr, du'a, halal and giving
156.howItsDone: Many Muslims shape each day around the five prayers, with dhikr after them, du'a throughout, attention to halal food and earning, and small acts of charity in between.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a thorny branch moved off a road, the lowest branch of faith and still a branch. Your line was clear the path. Today, the whole camp in one day. Day one hundred fifty-six.

I can do this. That was the promise of this camp, back on day ninety-seven, when it began with a single word: niyyah, the intention. Mean it first. Since then you've learned the prayer one movement at a time, learned how to start again, counted glory on your fingers, watched for a new moon, broken a fast with a date, stood at Arafah in your mind, asked with open hands, walked into a mosque, looked hard at what's halal, and given in a dozen small ways. So today, no new word. Just one ordinary day, from waking to sleep, with everything in it.
screen: `IT BEGAN WITH NIYYAH.` → `ONE MOVEMENT, ONE PRACTICE AT A TIME.` → `TODAY: ONE WHOLE DAY.`

segments.voice: It starts in the dark. Eyes open, and the first words are praise for being given life again. Taharah: wudu at the sink, slowly. Then the dawn prayer, facing the qiblah. Takbir. Qiyam. Ruku'. Sujud, closest when lowest. Tashahhud, then taslim, peace to both sides. Thirty-three, thirty-three, thirty-four on the fingers. Breakfast: bismillah, something halal and good. Then the day, which is most of it. Work, done honestly. A smile at the cashier, which is sadaqah. A stone moved from the road. At midday, the sun reaches its height and the day bows again: dhuhr. In the afternoon, asr. And in between, du'a, just asking, in any language, trusting, as the Qur'an says, that He is near. At sunset, maghrib. On the way home, something for the neighbor. At night, isha, and maybe, in the last prostration, the thing you've wanted to ask all day. Then before sleep: in Your name I die and I live. The Qur'an says, in Surah an-Nisa, that the prayer is prescribed for believers at fixed times. And Bukhari reports the Prophet ﷺ asking: if there were a river at your door and you bathed in it five times a day, would any dirt be left on you? That's the shape of the day this camp has built. Not one long act of worship. Five small returns, and everything in between leaning toward them. The next camp turns from practice to the text itself: the thirtieth part of the Qur'an, the short surahs most Muslims know by heart.
screen: `DAWN: WAKE, WASH, AND BOW.` · `THE DAY: CLEAN MONEY, A SMILE, A STONE.` · `NOON TO NIGHT: FIVE RETURNS.` · `A RIVER AT YOUR DOOR.` · then, large: `A DAY THAT BOWS.`

segments.voice: Picture tomorrow's five points, dawn, noon, midafternoon, sunset and night, and at each one a small pause: if you pray, the salat; if you don't, one quiet minute and one breath of thanks. Around them, place one smile, one clean deal, one thing moved from someone's way. Hold it all lightly.
Taharah, purification: the first step of a day that wove together the prayer, dhikr, the fast, du'a, the mosque, halal and giving.
Your line: a day that bows. From niyyah to here, one movement at a time. Camp three, complete.

157.title: Hearing before reading
157.hook: the Qur'an is first recited, heard, memorized, and only then read
157.howItsDone: Muslims learn the Qur'an by hearing it recited and repeating after a teacher, often memorizing before reading; many also listen to recordings of reciters.

segments.voice: Yesterday: taharah opened camp three's one whole day, five returns and everything leaning toward them. Your line was a day that bows. Day one hundred fifty-seven, and a new camp.

Nobody reads the lyrics of a lullaby. A child hears it in the dark, again and again, until one night the child sings it back. The words arrive through the ear. A mosque classroom on a Saturday morning works the same way: rows of kids, some rocking gently, repeating after a teacher, line by line, until the sound is in them. Some can recite whole surahs before they can read the script. This camp is about the text itself, and it starts where the text started: in the ear.
screen: `A SONG YOU NEVER READ.` → `KIDS REPEATING, LINE BY LINE.` → `THE TEXT STARTS IN THE EAR.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Muslim scholars connect the word Qur'an to a root meaning to read aloud, to recite: the Qur'an is the recitation. And tradition says the first word revealed, in a cave outside Mecca, was a command from that same root: iqra'. In Pickthall's translation, Surah al-Alaq opens: Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth. The Prophet ﷺ, Muslims say, could not read or write. So the Qur'an didn't arrive as a book. It arrived as sound, through the angel Jibril, a little at a time, over many years. The Prophet recited it; the companions heard and memorized it; some wrote it on whatever they had, palm stalks and thin flat stones. Bukhari reports that every Ramadan, Jibril went over all that had been revealed with him, aloud. Only after the Prophet's death was it gathered into a single written volume. The word for this reciting is tilawah. Arabic dictionaries give its root the sense of following, one thing after another, the way words follow words. And scholars point out a second meaning: to follow a text is also to live by it. To this day, the Qur'an is taught mouth to ear, teacher to student, in chains going back generation by generation. There are rules for how each letter is sounded, called tajwid. And a report in Abu Dawud says: beautify the Qur'an with your voices. The first listeners met it with their ears, not their eyes. For the next weeks, this camp walks through the thirtieth part, the last section, full of short surahs.
screen: `QUR'AN — THE RECITATION.` · `IQRA' — READ, RECITE.` · `SOUND FIRST, BOOK LATER.` · `TILAWAH — TO FOLLOW.` · then, large: `BEAUTIFY IT WITH YOUR VOICES.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen to the sounds already around you, the way you'd listen to music in a language you don't know yet: the rise and fall, the long vowels, the pauses. That's the ear a short surah asks for, al-Fatiha, al-Ikhlas or any of the last ones, heard from a reciter you like, without reading along or reaching for a translation yet.
Tilawah. Reciting the Qur'an aloud, from a root meaning to follow: word after word, and then in how you live. Today's word.
Your line: hear it first. The sound arrives first, and the meaning follows. Until tomorrow.

158.title: Seeking refuge first
158.hook: recitation begins with refuge from Shaytan, then bismillah (16:98)
158.howItsDone: Before reciting the Qur'an, Muslims usually say the ta'awwudh (a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim) and then, at the start of a surah, the bismillah; many also say the ta'awwudh when angry or troubled by a bad thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tilawah, the Qur'an heard before it's read. Your line was hear it first. Today, the two short lines said before a recitation begins. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

A reciter in front of a packed hall, or a nine-year-old at an evening class in Ohio: before the first verse, there are usually two short lines, the same two. Reciters say them the way a pilot runs the checklist before takeoff, quietly, as part of starting. The first line isn't from the surah at all. It's a request for protection. The second is the bismillah, which you met on day one. So why does a recitation start by asking for shelter, and only then say the name?
screen: `TWO LINES BEFORE THE FIRST VERSE.` → `THE SAME TWO, EACH TIME.` → `SHELTER FIRST.`

segments.voice: The first line is called the ta'awwudh, from a root that means to seek refuge, to run to someone for cover. The usual words are a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim: I seek refuge in Allah from Shaytan, the rejected one. The habit comes from a verse in Surah an-Nahl, which Pickthall translates: And when thou recitest the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from Satan the outcast. Jurists debated whether that makes it required or strongly recommended; either way, it became the habit before recitation. Why ask for protection right before something good? Some Muslim teachers say the moment you turn toward the good is exactly when distraction arrives. Someone opens the text and suddenly remembers an email. Someone stands to pray and replays an argument. Muslims understand Shaytan as a real being who whispers, and some also see his work in that ordinary pull away from what matters. Either way, the ta'awwudh is a door closing behind you before you sit down. Then comes the bismillah: in the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Scholars point to the order. First you let go of what you don't want to bring in; then you name what you're entering with. Clearing, then naming. And the ta'awwudh travels beyond recitation. A hadith in Bukhari tells of two men quarreling near the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, one red in the face with anger. The Prophet said he knew words that would make the anger leave: a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim. So people say it before reciting, and also in the middle of a bad moment, when a thought won't let go.
screen: `TA'AWWUDH — TO RUN FOR COVER.` · `SEEK REFUGE WHEN YOU RECITE (16:98).` · `CLEAR FIRST, THEN NAME.` · `WORDS FOR A HOT MOMENT.` · then, large: `REFUGE, THEN THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop. If you pray, say the two lines quietly, a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim, then bismillah ir-rahman ir-rahim; if you don't, follow the shape: name one thing pulling at you, and set it down on a long out-breath. Then stay in the quiet that comes after clearing and naming, without reciting or planning.
Ta'awwudh. Seeking refuge in Allah from Shaytan, the line said before reciting, just before the bismillah. Today's word.
Your line: refuge, then the name. The door closes before you sit down. That's one hundred fifty-eight days.

159.title: An-Nas: the people
159.hook: refuge with the Lord of people from the whisperer who withdraws (Surah 114)
159.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Surah an-Nas with al-Falaq and al-Ikhlas before sleep, blowing lightly into cupped hands and wiping them over the body, following the Prophet's practice; it is also recited after the prayers and for protection.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ta'awwudh, seeking refuge before reciting. Your line was refuge, then the name. Today, the Qur'an's very last surah. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

It's two in the morning. The house is quiet, and a voice in your head is not. You're not good enough. They were laughing at you. Check your phone one more time. It doesn't shout. It whispers, and it's very patient. The Qur'an's last surah, number one hundred fourteen, is about exactly this voice: six short lines, and a picture of the whisperer that surprises people. It sneaks in, and it slips away. Today the reading starts on the Qur'an's final page and works backward. Today: An-Nas, the people.
screen: `2AM, AND A VOICE THAT WHISPERS.` → `THE LAST SURAH OF THE QUR'AN.` → `READING FROM THE END.`

segments.voice: Pickthall translates the opening: Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind, The King of mankind, The God of mankind. Mankind, three times. In Arabic it's an-nas, the people, and every line of the surah ends on that sound: nas, nas, nas, then khannas, then nas twice more. Read aloud, it rocks like a lullaby. Allah is named three ways: Lord, the one who raises and cares for you; King, the one in charge; God, the one who is worshipped. Three doors to the same refuge. The danger is named once, in two words: al-waswas al-khannas. Waswas is the whisper, a word that sounds like what it means. Khannas means the one who draws back, who shrinks away and hides. Commentators explain the picture: the whisperer comes when you forget Allah, and retreats when you remember Him. In that picture, the whisper can't hold its ground against remembrance; it works best unnoticed. The surah ends by saying the whisperers come from among the jinn and from among people. Some of the voices that pull you down are unseen. Some have phone numbers. Aisha reports in Bukhari that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had a habit with these last surahs: every night before sleep he would cup his hands, recite al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and an-Nas into them, and wipe his hands over his body, three times. So for Muslims who keep that habit, the last page of the book is also the last thing said before the lights go out.
screen: `LORD, KING, GOD — THREE DOORS.` · `WASWAS — THE WHISPER.` · `KHANNAS — THE ONE WHO DRAWS BACK.` · `THE LAST WORDS BEFORE SLEEP.` · then, large: `THE WHISPERER WITHDRAWS.`

segments.voice: Let one recent whisper come to mind, the kind that sounds like your own voice but isn't kind, and don't argue with it; just name it: that's a whisper. If you pray, you can say the surah's first line, qul a'udhu bi rabbin-nas, and let it be the remembering. Then watch what the whisper does when it's looked at directly.

Your line: the whisperer withdraws. Lord, King, God: three doors to one refuge. One hundred fifty-nine, in the books.

160.title: Al-Falaq: the daybreak
160.hook: refuge with the Lord of the dawn from darkness, knots and envy (Surah 113)
160.howItsDone: Muslims who keep the morning and evening remembrances recite al-Falaq with an-Nas and al-Ikhlas three times each morning and evening, and also after the prayers and before sleep, following the hadith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: An-Nas, the last surah, and the whisperer who draws back when Allah is remembered. Your line was the whisperer withdraws. Today, its twin. Day one hundred sixty.

Before dawn, for a long time, it's simply dark. Then a thin gray line opens along the horizon, like a seam splitting, and the night that felt endless turns out to have an edge. Yesterday's surah was about the danger inside, the whisper. Its twin, the surah just before it, is about dangers from outside: the dark, harm done in secret, other people's envy. And it names the One it turns to in a striking way. Not the Lord of the night. The Lord of the break.
screen: `A GRAY LINE ON THE HORIZON.` → `THE NIGHT HAS AN EDGE.` → `THE LORD OF THE BREAK.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred thirteen opens, in Pickthall's translation: Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the Daybreak. Falaq comes from a root meaning to split. The same root describes a seed splitting open to sprout, and the dawn splitting the dark. So the first thing the surah tells you about the One you run to is that He breaks the night open. Then it names four things to seek refuge from. First, the evil in what He created, a general line covering anything that can go wrong in a created world. Second, the darkness when it settles in, the night, and everything that feels bigger in it. Third, those who blow on knots. Commentators explain this as sorcery, the practice of tying knots and breathing spells on them. Classical scholars held that such harm is real and Allah's protection greater; some modern readers take the knots more figuratively. Fourth, the envier when he envies. Scholars define this envy as more than wanting what someone has: it's wanting them not to have it. The surah doesn't ask you to fight any of these yourself. It asks you to say: I seek refuge. An-Nas and Al-Falaq together are called al-mu'awwidhatan, the two refuge surahs. A hadith of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says that reciting them with al-Ikhlas three times in the morning and three in the evening is enough protection for everything. Yesterday's surah went with him into sleep. This one's name makes it easy to pair with first light, though the hadith keeps both for morning and evening alike.
screen: `FALAQ — TO SPLIT, LIKE A SEED OR DAWN.` · `FOUR THINGS TO SEEK REFUGE FROM.` · `ENVY — WANTING THEM NOT TO HAVE IT.` · `THE TWO REFUGE SURAHS.` · then, large: `LORD OF THE DAYBREAK.`

segments.voice: Picture the first gray light of a dawn you've seen, and hold it. Then bring in one thing about the day ahead that feels like the dark, a meeting, a worry, a person who wishes you ill, and without solving it, set it in front of the light. If you pray, you can say the first line: qul a'udhu bi rabbil-falaq.
Al-Falaq. The daybreak, from a root meaning to split open, the name of Surah one hundred thirteen. Today's word.
Your line: lord of the daybreak. Even the longest night has an edge. One hundred sixty days now.

161.title: Al-Ikhlas: sincerity
161.hook: say, He is Allah, One, the Eternal, unbegotten, none like Him (Surah 112)
161.tomorrow: Worth a third of the Qur'an
161.howItsDone: Surah al-Ikhlas is among the first surahs Muslim children learn; it is recited often in the daily prayers, three times with al-Falaq and an-Nas morning and evening, and before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Falaq, the daybreak, and refuge in the One who splits the dark. Your line was lord of the daybreak. Day one hundred sixty-one.

In the car, with no warning, a child asks the biggest question there is: what is God like? Where did God come from? Who are God's parents? According to the commentators, people asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ questions like these. Describe your Lord to us. What is He made of? Where is He from? The answer came as one of the shortest surahs in the Qur'an. Four lines. It fits on an index card, and Muslim children often learn it right after al-Fatiha.
screen: `WHAT IS GOD LIKE?` → `DESCRIBE YOUR LORD TO US.` → `FOUR LINES.`

segments.voice: Here is Surah one hundred twelve, in Pickthall's translation: Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him. You've heard its key word twice on this path, from Bilal on the burning sand, on day fifteen and day ninety-one. Qul huwa Allahu ahad. Arabic has two words for one. Wahid is one in a count, the first number. Ahad is one with no second at all: it can't be split, copied or added to. Then as-samad. Pickthall reaches for eternally Besought of all. Scholars give it layers: the one everyone turns to in need, who needs no one; the one who is complete, without a hollow. Then two denials: no children, no parents. God is not part of a family tree. And last: nothing is like Him, nothing you can picture, compare or draw. None of these lines says ikhlas. It means sincerity, or purity, the way you'd purify gold of anything mixed in. Scholars say the surah is named for what it does: it makes belief in the one God pure. That oneness is called tawhid, the center of Islamic belief. Jews and Christians also confess one God, and Christians understand that oneness through the Trinity; this surah is how Muslims say it, in their own four lines. And that closes a week: the stone lifted from the road, the close of the practices camp, then the text camp opening with hear it first, refuge first, and three surahs of refuge and oneness.
screen: `SAY: HE IS ALLAH, THE ONE.` · `AHAD — ONE WITH NO SECOND.` · `AS-SAMAD — NEEDED BY ALL.` · `NONE COMPARABLE UNTO HIM.` · then, large: `HE IS ONE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, you can recite the surah three times, slowly, qul huwa Allahu ahad, all four lines, with a breath between rounds. If you don't, let your mind reach for a picture of the biggest thing you know, the night sky, the ocean, the whole of time, and notice how fast it comes. Then remember the last line, none is comparable, set the picture down, and sit in the space it leaves.
Ahad. One, with no second: the oneness of Allah in the first line of Surah al-Ikhlas. Today's word.
Your line: he is one. One, with no second, and nothing mixed in. See you tomorrow.
